region: Eastern China — ponds, lakes & slow rivers; feral worldwide
description: The wild goldfish is an olive-bronze, carp-like fish; Chinese fish-keepers began breeding its rare orange mutants in ponds more than a thousand years ago. Even domestic goldfish fry start out this bronze colour and only turn orange as they grow.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: eastern China)
description: The original single-tailed domestic goldfish, a hardy pond fish that can pass 30 cm and live over 20 years given space. It forages constantly, sifting gravel and uprooting soft plants.

region: Captive-bred, USA (wild form: eastern China)
description: A single-tailed breed developed in the United States in the late 1800s, with a deeply forked tail that can match its body length. The fastest and most agile goldfish, it belongs in ponds or very large tanks.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: eastern China)
description: A red-and-white comet: the long, deeply forked tail of the comet with bold red patches on a white body. The red areas can spread or fade as the fish matures.

region: Captive-bred, UK (wild form: eastern China)
description: A calico single-tail with the short fins of a common goldfish. Its mix of transparent and reflective scales lets blue, red, orange and black patches show through like a mosaic.

region: Captive-bred, UK (wild form: eastern China)
description: Standardised by the Bristol Aquarists’ Society in the 1930s for its large, rounded, heart-shaped tail. Prized fish show a blue base mottled with violet, red and black.

region: Captive-bred, Japan (wild form: eastern China)
description: Japan’s oldest goldfish breed: a twin tail on the long, streamlined body of a common goldfish. Hardy and fast, it is a traditional pond fish, usually red-and-white.

region: Captive-bred, Aichi Prefecture, Japan
description: A rare breed from the Nagoya area whose twin tail spreads into an X shape when seen from behind. Show-standard fish are white with red confined to the lips and fins.

region: Captive-bred, Japan (wild form: eastern China)
description: A Meiji-era Japanese cross of wakin and ryukin that pairs a slim, hardy body with a long, flowing twin tail. It is still raised in outdoor ponds in Japan.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: eastern China)
description: An egg-shaped goldfish with a split, twin caudal and anal fin. It is the Western counterpart of the ryukin without the shoulder hump, and one of the hardiest fancy breeds.

region: Captive-bred, Japan (wild form: eastern China)
description: Named after the Ryukyu Islands, through which its ancestors reached Japan from China. It is known for the steep hump rising behind the head and a long, flowing double tail.

region: Captive-bred, Kochi (Tosa) Prefecture, Japan
description: A rare breed from Kochi whose huge twin tail is joined at the top and spreads sideways with curled-forward edges. It is bred to be viewed from above, traditionally raised in shallow round bowls because it swims weakly.

region: Captive-bred, USA (wild form: eastern China)
description: Developed in Philadelphia in the 1890s: a rounded body with a tall dorsal and a long, square-edged double tail that hangs like a veil. It is difficult to breed true and rare in today’s trade.

region: Captive-bred, Yamagata Prefecture, Japan
description: A Yamagata breed with the round, humped body of a ryukin but a long single "mackerel" tail. It was bred to survive cold northern winters in outdoor ponds.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: eastern China)
description: A dorsal-finned twin-tail with a raspberry-like hood (wen) of fatty tissue over the head. The wen keeps growing for years and can cover the eyes if left unchecked.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: eastern China)
description: A white oranda whose only red is the hood on top of its head. The cap is often well developed, while the cheeks and gill covers stay white.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: eastern China)
description: A steel-blue to slate-grey colour strain of the oranda. The colour comes from dark pigment under reflective scales and often warms toward bronze as the fish ages.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: eastern China)
description: A deep chocolate-brown colour strain of the oranda, usually with a lighter, bronze-toned hood and belly. The brown can lighten toward orange with age.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: eastern China)
description: A Chinese breed with no dorsal fin and a full hood over the cheeks and crown, said to recall a Chinese guardian lion. It is the ancestor of the Japanese ranchu.

region: Captive-bred, Japan (wild form: eastern China)
description: Called the "king of goldfish" in Japan: no dorsal fin, a hooded head and a deeply arched back that curves into a short tail held at a downward angle. Ranchu are judged from above.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: eastern China)
description: A velvety black telescope-eyed twin-tail. Its protruding eyes give it poor vision, and the black can fade to bronze or orange with age or in warm water.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: eastern China)
description: An orange-red telescope goldfish with eyes bulging on short stalks, called demekin ("protruding-eye goldfish") in Japan. The eyes start normal in fry and protrude over the first months.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: eastern China)
description: The black-and-white colour type of the telescope goldfish. Like most black goldfish, its black patches can recede over the years.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: eastern China)
description: A telescope-eyed breed whose wide twin tail spreads flat like butterfly wings when seen from above. It is usually seen in black-and-white (panda) or calico.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: eastern China)
description: A dorsal-less Chinese breed whose telescopic eyes point permanently upward. The eyes are normal in young fry and rotate skyward as the fish grows.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: eastern China)
description: A dorsal-less breed with large fluid-filled sacs under its upturned eyes that wobble as it swims. The sacs puncture easily, so it needs smooth décor and gentle filtration.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: eastern China)
description: Each scale is domed by a raised calcium deposit, giving the body a pearl-studded look. The near-spherical body makes it a slow, clumsy swimmer that needs a calm tank.

region: Captive-bred, Japan (wild form: eastern China)
description: A Japanese pearlscale line topped by a soft, bubble-like hood on the crown of the head. Like all pearlscales it has domed, pearl-like scales and a round body.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: eastern China)
description: Named for the fleshy bundles of nasal tissue (narial bouquets) that grow from the nostrils and sway as it swims. Large pompoms can be sucked into the mouth while it feeds.

region: Europe — weedy ponds, lakes & oxbows from England to Siberia
description: A deep-bodied wild relative of the goldfish that survives months without oxygen under winter ice by turning lactic acid into ethanol. Where pike are present it grows a taller body that is harder to swallow.

region: East Asia — Amur basin south through China to northern Vietnam
description: The wild East Asian carp from which Niigata rice farmers bred koi in the early 1800s; it is now usually treated as a species distinct from the European common carp. Wild fish are slimmer than farmed carp, bronze-olive above with reddish-tinged lower fins.

region: Europe & Central Asia — Danube, Black, Caspian & Aral Sea basins; introduced worldwide
description: A powerful bottom-feeder that sucks up mud with protrusible lips and sifts it for food, clouding the water as it goes. Carp were raised in ponds by the Romans and by medieval monasteries.

region: Captive-bred, central Europe (wild form: Danube basin)
description: A domesticated scale mutant of the common carp, bred in central European fish farms for centuries, with only a few large, irregular mirror-like scales along the back and lateral line. Crossing it with Japanese koi produced the doitsu koi varieties.

region: Captive-bred, Niigata, Japan (wild form: Amur carp, East Asia)
description: The foundational koi variety, fixed in Niigata in the late 1800s: a snow-white body with red (hi) patterns. Judges look for crisp pattern edges and a clean white nose and tail joint.

region: Captive-bred, Niigata, Japan (wild form: Amur carp, East Asia)
description: A three-coloured koi first exhibited in the Taishō era (1910s): a kohaku pattern with small black (sumi) patches on the back, but never on the head. Fine black stripes often mark the tail and dorsal fin.

region: Captive-bred, Niigata, Japan (wild form: Amur carp, East Asia)
description: A black-based three-colour koi first produced in 1927, early in the Shōwa era: wrapping black (sumi) with red and white, including black on the head. The pectoral fins carry black at their bases (motoguro).

region: Captive-bred, Niigata, Japan (wild form: Amur carp, East Asia)
description: A pure white koi whose only red is a single round spot on the head, echoing the red-crowned crane (tancho) and the Japanese flag. The spot cannot be bred for reliably, so good tancho are scarce.

region: Captive-bred, Niigata, Japan (wild form: Amur carp, East Asia)
description: A single-coloured metallic gold koi; ogon were first fixed by Sawata Aoki in the 1940s, and the Yamabuki line is named after the yellow kerria flower. Its shine makes it easy to spot in a dark pond.

region: Captive-bred, Niigata, Japan (wild form: Amur carp, East Asia)
description: A solid metallic white-silver ogon (purachina) with a polished, chrome-like sheen. Its plain colour shows off the fine, even scale net that judges look for.

region: Captive-bred, Niigata, Japan (wild form: Amur carp, East Asia)
description: A solid metallic orange ogon whose colour deepens on carotenoid-rich food. Like other ogon, it tends to grow quickly and boldly approaches people at the pond edge.

region: Captive-bred, Niigata, Japan (wild form: Amur carp, East Asia)
description: One of the oldest koi, descended from the indigo-backed asagi magoi: a blue-grey back covered in a net of pale-edged scales, with red-orange cheeks, flanks and fin bases.

region: Captive-bred, Niigata, Japan (wild form: Amur carp, East Asia)
description: A doitsu (nearly scaleless) asagi created around 1910 by Yoshigoro Akiyama by crossing asagi with German mirror carp. A row of large dark-blue scales runs along each side of the dorsal fin above red flanks.

region: Captive-bred, Niigata, Japan (wild form: Amur carp, East Asia)
description: A tea-brown, non-metallic koi famed as the tamest and fastest-growing variety. It is often first to feed from the hand, so keepers add one to coax shy koi to the surface.

region: Captive-bred, Niigata, Japan (wild form: Amur carp, East Asia)
description: A plain, non-metallic sky-grey koi with a fine net of pale scale edges. Like chagoi it is very tame and grows large.

region: Captive-bred, Niigata, Japan (wild form: Amur carp, East Asia)
description: A grey-blue koi with copper-brown patches, its name meaning "autumn leaves falling on water". It comes from soragoi × chagoi lines and shares their gentle, fast-growing nature.

region: Captive-bred, Niigata, Japan (wild form: Amur carp, East Asia)
description: A solid deep red-orange, non-metallic koi, usually selected from kohaku spawnings that lack white. Its colour is strongest on carotenoid-rich food.

region: Captive-bred, Niigata, Japan (wild form: Amur carp, East Asia)
description: A mustard-yellow, non-metallic koi; it is among the largest-growing and friendliest varieties. Its body often has a pale, reticulated scale net.

region: Captive-bred, Niigata, Japan (wild form: Amur carp, East Asia)
description: A red koi in which every scale has a dark centre, forming a pinecone (matsuba) net over the back. The net is sharpest in cool water.

region: Captive-bred, Niigata, Japan (wild form: Amur carp, East Asia)
description: A black koi with snow-white patterning; utsuri means "reflections". The black wraps around the body and onto the head, and the pectoral fins carry black at the base.

region: Captive-bred, Niigata, Japan (wild form: Amur carp, East Asia)
description: A black koi with red-orange patterning in place of the white of shiro utsuri. Young fish often show patchy black that firms up as they grow.

region: Captive-bred, Niigata, Japan (wild form: Amur carp, East Asia)
description: The yellow-patterned member of the utsuri group: deep wrapping black with lemon-yellow areas, including yellow on the head. It is rarer in ponds than shiro or hi utsuri.

region: Captive-bred, Niigata, Japan (wild form: Amur carp, East Asia)
description: A doitsu koi whose name means "dragon in the clouds". Its black-and-white pattern can change dramatically with season and water temperature, sometimes turning almost all black or all white.

region: Captive-bred, Niigata, Japan (wild form: Amur carp, East Asia)
description: A white koi with small stepping-stone black spots along the back and none on the head — essentially a sanke without red. Clean white skin is as important as the sumi placement.

region: Captive-bred, Niigata, Japan (wild form: Amur carp, East Asia)
description: Goshiki means "five colours": a kohaku-style red pattern over a white base netted with blue and black scale edges. The net darkens in cool water and lightens in summer.

region: Captive-bred, Niigata, Japan (wild form: Amur carp, East Asia)
description: Kujaku ("peacock") is a metallic koi with a platinum base, a dark pinecone (matsuba) net over the back and red-orange patches. It was developed in Japan in the 1960s.

region: Captive-bred, USA & Japan (from koi × Indonesian long-finned carp)
description: Long-finned koi from crosses of koi with Indonesian long-finned river carp, popularised in the 1980s. Their flowing fins and barbels keep growing for years, and they come in all the standard koi colours.

region: Chao Phraya basin, Thailand — critically endangered in the wild
description: A velvet-black minnow with a blood-red tail, now critically endangered in its native Thai rivers; aquarium fish are farm-bred. Adults defend a cave or stretch of bottom fiercely against fish of similar shape or colour.

region: Mekong, Chao Phraya & Mae Klong basins — Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam
description: A grey-blue bottom-dweller with bright red fins and a dark "bridle" from snout to eye, from sandy-bottomed rivers that flood seasonally. It chases fish of similar shape away from its patch, so only one should be kept per tank.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Mekong & Chao Phraya basins)
description: An albino line of the rainbow shark: pinkish-white body, red eyes and the same scarlet fins. It is just as territorial as the wild-coloured form.

region: Captive-bred, USA — genetically modified (wild form: Mekong basin)
description: A rainbow shark carrying a fluorescent-protein gene from a marine organism, so it glows vivid orange under blue light. Its behaviour is identical to the wild form, including territoriality.

region: Captive-bred, USA — genetically modified (wild form: Mekong basin)
description: A genetically modified rainbow shark with a purple, fluorescent body that glows under blue light, keeping the species’ red fins. It is as territorial as an ordinary rainbow shark.

region: Malay Peninsula, Sumatra & Borneo — forest streams
description: Rests propped on its pectoral and pelvic fins on rock and wood, rasping off biofilm. A gold line above its black side stripe and black-and-white banded fins set it apart from the Siamese algae eater.

region: Mekong & Chao Phraya basins, Malay Peninsula, Sumatra & Borneo — large rivers and lakes
description: A big-eyed, torpedo-shaped schooling minnow with silver scales and black-edged, yellowish fins. Skittish and a powerful jumper, it grows large and needs a long, covered tank; aquarium fish are farmed.

region: Mekong & Chao Phraya basins, Malay Peninsula & Indonesia — large rivers and floodplains
description: A Southeast Asian river giant that can pass 80 cm in the wild. Juveniles are sold as velvet-black "black sharks" but grow into territorial bottom-grazers that need a very large aquarium.

region: Turkey, Syria, Iraq & Iran — Tigris–Euphrates streams and hot springs
description: Famous as the "doctor fish" of Turkish hot springs, where it nibbles dead skin from bathers. It uses a sucking disc on its lower lip to graze biofilm in fast streams.

region: Rakhine Yoma, western Myanmar — fast, rocky hill streams
description: A small hillstream Garra banded black and yellow like a bumblebee. It grazes biofilm from stones in fast, oxygen-rich water and squabbles harmlessly with its own kind over grazing spots.

region: Mekong & Chao Phraya basins, Malay Peninsula, Sumatra & Borneo — clear, flowing streams
description: Grazes algae from every surface and is one of few fish that eat black brush algae. Its jagged-edged black stripe runs all the way into the tail fork, which separates it from look-alike flying foxes.

region: Mekong & Chao Phraya basins — Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam
description: Despite its name it comes from Indochina, not China. An extra gill opening above each gill cover lets it breathe while its sucker mouth stays clamped to rock in fast water; large adults may latch onto slow, flat-sided tankmates.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Mekong & Chao Phraya basins)
description: A xanthic, golden-yellow line of the Chinese algae eater that has lost the dark stripe and speckling. It has the same sucker mouth, extra gill openings and grumpy adult temperament.

region: Sumatra & Borneo — rivers that flood the forest seasonally
description: A long-lived, sociable loach that clicks audibly when feeding or squabbling and often rests lying on its side, alarming new owners. It eats snails eagerly and grows far larger and older than most buyers expect.

region: Northern India & Nepal — Ganges basin foothill rivers
description: Juveniles’ dark markings spell out "Y-O-Y-O" along the flank, which gave the trade name; with age the pattern breaks into a lacy net. Often sold as the "Pakistani loach", it actually comes from northern India and Nepal.

region: Ganges & Brahmaputra basins — India, Bangladesh & Nepal
description: A yellowish loach with dark Y-shaped bars that subdivide into a net as it ages. Like other botiids it carries an erectile spine below each eye for defence.

region: Ataran basin, Myanmar–Thailand border — clear, rocky hill rivers
description: Described only in 2004, this loach has a dark body laced with pale greenish-yellow bands and dots that grow more intricate with age. It is one of the more peaceful Botia and very active in a group.

region: Western Ghats, India — clear, fast streams in Maharashtra & Karnataka
description: From streams of India’s Western Ghats, its many thin green-brown bars separated by pale yellow lines give a zebra look. It is one of the most peaceful Botia and suits community tanks.

region: Brahmaputra & Ganges basins — India, Bangladesh & Bhutan
description: Bright yellow with six or seven broad, slanting dark bars, a lively loach of clear foothill rivers. It is easily confused with the Burmese Botia histrionica.

region: Myanmar — Irrawaddy & Sittang basins
description: A Myanmar loach with broad black bands across a golden-yellow body, often sold mixed with the similar B. dario. Like other botiids it probes the substrate with its barbels and squeezes into tight crevices to rest.

region: Ganges & Brahmaputra basins — India, Bangladesh & Nepal
description: Its intricate net of dark lines and bars over a yellowish body is often likened to a ladder. It is frequently confused with B. lohachata and B. almorhae in the trade.

region: Mekong & Chao Phraya basins, northern Malay Peninsula
description: A blue-grey loach with bright orange-red fins. It becomes boisterous and territorial with age and is best kept in a group so that aggression is spread out.

region: Mekong, Chao Phraya & Mae Klong basins — Thailand, Laos, Cambodia
description: Named for the thin black stripe along its back from snout to tail, plus a dark bar at the tail base. It is feisty and quarrelsome for its size.

region: Mekong & Chao Phraya basins — Thailand, Laos, Cambodia
description: A silvery-green loach with orange-tinged fins and a dark blotch at the tail base. Like its relative the blue botia, it gets more territorial as it grows.

region: Mae Klong & Chao Phraya basins, Thailand — endangered in the wild
description: One of the smallest botiids, it shoals in mid-water rather than hugging the bottom. Wild populations have declined sharply after dam building, and the trade now relies on farm-bred fish.

region: Upper Mekong — Yunnan (China) & northern Laos
description: Two black lines run from snout to tail on a cream body; with age they break up into a more complex pattern. A small, sociable loach described in 1987.

region: Myanmar & western Thailand — Irrawaddy, Sittang & Salween basins
description: A large, chunky loach with about a dozen thin dark bars and rows of spots over a greenish-gold body, and orange fins dotted with black. It can be belligerent and needs plenty of caves.

region: Malay Peninsula, Sumatra & Borneo — flowing forest rivers
description: Greenish-gold with 11–15 narrow blue-black bars, a fast, territorial loach. It needs a long tank with caves and current, and is best kept with robust tankmates.

region: Mekong & Chao Phraya basins — Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam
description: The largest and most aggressive of the commonly sold botiids: golden-green with broad blue-black bars and a red-orange tail. It should be kept in a group in a large tank with tankmates that can hold their own.

region: Southern China (Guangxi, Guangdong) & northern Vietnam — upland streams
description: A subtropical loach whose dark bars are broken up by a net of yellow-orange lines. It tolerates cooler water than most botiids and can be territorial toward its own kind.
